title: The Association Between Running Injuries and Training Parameters: A Systematic Review
authors: Fredette A, Roy JS, Perreault K, Dupuis F, Napier C, Esculier JF
population: Runners across 36 studies with prospective data (novice, recreational and competitive); searches to 7 July 2020
findings: 36 articles with 23,047 runners; 6043 (26.2%) had a running-related injury (range 8.8% to 91.3%).
Incidence was 14.9% in novice runners (range 9.4-94.9%), 26.1% in recreational (17.9-79.3%) and 62.6% in competitive runners (52.6-91.3%).
Most frequent sites were the knee (25.8%), foot/ankle (24.4%) and lower leg (24.4%).

Evidence on the association between weekly distance, duration, frequency, intensity or specific changes in training parameters and injury was conflicting; the authors advise caution when recommending optimal parameters or progressions.
limitations: Heterogeneous definitions of injury and exposure; the review cannot say whether 3 x 20 versus 3 x 30 or a ramp exemption is safer; the novice incidence range is very wide.
implications: No training parameter is reliably linked to injury, so the ramp exemption for the floor week and the choice of 3 x 20 versus 3 x 30 cannot be derived from outcome evidence; they are D-grade defaults.
Use a graded, conservative start because novices carry a pooled 14.9% injury incidence, without claiming a numeric optimum.

No progression threshold in the engine (10%/week soft, 30% over 2 weeks hard) can be graded above C/D on this review; label the weekly ramp rules as conventions with low-certainty evidence, not as findings.
Display progression limits as cautions, not as medical limits, and avoid copy implying a safe or unsafe number.
Novice incidence in the pooled data is lower than competitive incidence, which probably reflects exposure and follow-up differences (an inference); do not read it as novices tolerating faster ramps.
Do not present a long-run cap as injury-evidence-backed; justify any cap by convention (Daniels, Higdon, Johnson) and label it a default (grade D).
Prefer gradual, rating-informed progression over fixed hard thresholds; the evidence does not identify a safe or unsafe single-session duration.

verification.notes: Re-fetched Crossref (J Athl Train, first author Fredette, online 2021-09-03) and Europe PMC abstract (PMID 34478518; journal year 2022). All numbers match. Removed 'even on supervised programmes' from an implication: the abstract does not say the novice studies were supervised.
